outcomes.goal: Name core home spaces and locate a person or object inside one.

models.title: Start with the home
models.note: Butas is a flat or apartment. Kambarys is a room; virtuvė is a kitchen. First learn the names, then use their location forms.

models.title: One person, three locations
models.note: A location needs no preposition: butas → bute, kambarys → kambaryje, virtuvė → virtuvėje. Virtuvėje follows the same pattern as kavinėje in the previous chapter.

outcomes.goal: Distinguish presence from absence and change the noun after nėra.

models.title: Keep the object the same
models.note: Yra uses the naming form stalas. Nėra uses stalo, the genitive. The missing object is still a table; the sentence changes its form.

models.title: The same contrast with a chair
models.note: With a noun ending in -ė, the absent-object form ends in -ės: kėdė → kėdės.

models.title: Ask about a facility
models.note: Ar makes a yes/no question. Internetas stays in its naming form after yra. After nėra, use interneto, just as stalas becomes stalo.

models.title: A feminine noun ending in -ia
models.note: Vonia becomes vonios after nėra. Compare lova → lovos: both end in -os, but keep the i in vonios.

models.title: A noun ending in -ius
models.note: Televizorius becomes televizoriaus. This -ius → -iaus change differs from stalas → stalo.

outcomes.goal: Use plural naming forms and selected d→dž / t→č stem changes.

models.title: The plural forms
models.note: For these naming forms: -as becomes -ai, -ė becomes -ės, and -ys becomes -iai. Kėdės can also mean of a chair after nėra; the surrounding sentence tells you its role.

models.title: Tree: plural naming and counting forms
models.note: The naming plural is medžiai; the counting form after kiek is medžių. Both change d to dž.

models.title: A dormitory
models.note: Bendrabutis changes t to č: bendrabučio after nėra, bendrabučiai as a plural naming form. You saw the same stem change in rankšluostis → rankšluosčio.

models.title: Mirror: change the ending and stem
models.note: Veidrodis ends in -is. Its genitive is veidrodžio: d changes to dž before -io. Compare the chair form kėdžių you already learned.

checks.translation: There is no mirror in the room.

checks.hint: Check what the sentence needs to say. You can open the example for help.
checks.correction: Like du, trys takes the plural naming form: bendrabučiai.

outcomes.goal: Match number gender and contrast naming plurals after two with genitive plurals after ten/kiek.

models.title: Two has two forms
models.note: Stalas and kambarys are masculine, so use du. Kėdė is feminine, so use dvi. The number still means two; the noun determines its form.

models.title: The question and the answer use different forms
models.note: When asking how many rooms, use kiek + genitive plural: kambarių. In the answer, du takes the plural naming form kambariai.

models.title: One object
models.note: One agrees with a singular noun: vienas stalas, viena kėdė. For two or more, use the plural forms you learned earlier.

models.title: Three uses the same number form
models.note: Trys is the same for these masculine and feminine nouns. The nouns are still plural.

models.title: Five agrees with the noun
models.note: Penki goes with masculine stalai; penkios with feminine kėdės. Four and six through nine also have separate masculine and feminine forms, introduced in the next lessons.

models.title: The number changes the noun form
models.note: Two takes the plural naming form kėdės. Ten and kiek take genitive plural kėdžių. Notice the changed stem d → dž. This is a form contrast, not an optional spelling difference.

models.title: Many and few use the same case
models.note: Daug means many and mažai means few. Both take genitive plural, just like kiek and dešimt.

outcomes.goal: Ask for a floor location and distinguish it from a room number.

models.title: Naming the floor
models.note: Both words change for a location: pirmas aukštas → pirmame aukšte.

models.title: Which floor?
models.note: The question and answer both use location forms: kelintame aukšte / antrame aukšte. Antras becomes antrame.

models.title: Two different questions
models.note: A room number names the room: dvyliktas kambarys. A floor location uses kelintame aukšte, with both words in the location form. Dvyliktas means twelfth, used here to identify room twelve.

checks.translation: The kitchen is on the second floor.
checks.hint: Check what the sentence needs to say. You can open the example for help.
checks.correction: The floor location uses antrame aukšte.

outcomes.goal: Agree adjectives and description questions with masculine/feminine nouns.

models.title: The same adjective with two nouns
models.note: Butas is masculine; virtuvė is feminine. The adjective agrees: didelis / didelė. Both mean large.

models.title: A second adjective pattern
models.note: For mažas, the feminine is maža. Learn the paired forms: didelis / didelė, mažas / maža.

models.title: Ask about the flat or kitchen
models.note: Koks asks about masculine butas; kokia asks about feminine virtuvė. These questions ask for a description, not a location.

models.title: New: -as and -a
models.note: Naujas / nauja follows the same pairing as mažas / maža. Keep the meaning new and match the noun’s gender.

models.title: Cosy: -us and -i
models.note: Jaukus has the feminine form jauki. The feminine form does not always end in -a: learn the paired forms, not one universal ending.

models.title: Bright follows the same pairing
models.note: Šviesus / šviesi follows the same -us / -i pairing as jaukus / jauki.

outcomes.goal: Use ant/prie/tarp/vidury with familiar objects and genitive forms.

models.title: One table, two positions
models.note: Ant means on; prie means beside. Both take stalo, the same genitive form you used after nėra. The preposition changes the position, not the noun form.

models.title: Use a second familiar object
pairs: The chair is by the window.
models.note: Langas becomes lango after prie, just as stalas becomes stalo.

models.title: Between two objects
pairs: Between the table and the bed.
Kėdė yra tarp stalo ir lovos.
The chair is between the table and the bed.
models.note: Tarp means between. Both objects use genitive: stalas → stalo, lova → lovos. Ir joins them.

models.title: Inside or in the middle
pairs: The table is in the room.
The table is in the middle of the room.
models.note: Kambaryje says in the room. Vidury kambario specifies the middle; kambarys takes genitive kambario after vidury.

checks.correction: Both objects after tarp are genitive.

outcomes.goal: Distinguish a needed object from a needed action, and wanting from having to act.

models.title: The same object, two messages
models.note: Both nėra and reikia take the genitive kompiuterio. Adding man says who needs it: I do. The noun form stays the same.

models.title: A towel
models.note: Rankšluostis becomes rankšluosčio: t changes to č before -io. Learn this exact form with the noun; do not just remove its ending.

models.title: The need can be an action
pairs: The window needs to be closed.
models.note: A needed object uses genitive: kompiuterio. A needed action uses an infinitive: uždaryti. The action still has its own object, langą.

models.title: Want to or have to
pairs: I want to tidy the room.
I have to tidy the room.
models.note: Tvarkyti means to tidy. Noriu expresses a wish; turiu + infinitive expresses an obligation. Keep tvarkyti kambarį the same and change only the meaning of the first verb.

checks.translation: I have to close the window.
checks.hint: Check what the sentence needs to say. You can open the example for help.

checks.translation: A computer is needed in the kitchen.
checks.hint: Check what the sentence needs to say. You can open the example for help.

outcomes.limit: New-context checks sample obligation and noun need; infinitive need is practised with repeated bounded prompts.

outcomes.goal: Ask permission for one's own action versus asking another person politely.

models.title: Open the window
models.note: Atidaryti and uždaryti are infinitives: to open and to close. Langas becomes langą as the object of the action.

models.title: Who will do the action?
models.note: Galiu means I can; galite addresses you politely. The action atidaryti stays unchanged. Ar galiu asks permission for your own action; ar galite asks the other person to act.

checks.translation: May I close the window?
checks.hint: Check what the sentence needs to say. You can open the example for help.
checks.correction: Ask permission for your own action with galiu.

checks.translation: Can you close the window? (polite)
checks.hint: Check what the sentence needs to say. You can open the example for help.
checks.correction: Ask the other person to act with polite galite.

checks.translation: Can you help (formal)?
checks.hint: Use the meaning and surrounding words to choose the form.
checks.correction: Galite addresses someone politely; galiu means I can.

outcomes.goal: Report missing hot water and ask for help with a repair.

models.title: Hot water: present or absent
models.note: After nėra, both words change: karštas vanduo → karšto vandens. Learn vandens with vanduo; it does not follow the table or chair endings.

models.title: Ask for and offer help
models.note: Pagalba becomes pagalbos after reikia. Padėti means to help: galite asks the other person; galiu offers your own help.

models.title: A useful response
pairs: We need to call a plumber.
models.note: Kviesti can mean to invite or to call someone in. Santechnikas becomes santechniką as the person to call. Reikia is followed by the infinitive kviesti.

models.title: A short repair message
pairs: He will be here in the afternoon.
models.note: Gal softens the request. Kviečiu says I am calling. Learn bus po pietų as a useful future-time message here; the wider future-tense pattern comes later.

models.title: The question and the answer use different forms

models.title: Which floor?

models.title: Ask about a facility
models.note: Ar makes a yes/no question. Internetas stays in its naming form after yra. After nėra, use interneto, just as stalas becomes stalo.

models.title: Ask what the rent costs
models.note: You used kiek kainuoja to ask prices at a café. Use the same question for rent. Here nuoma is what costs money, so it stays in its naming form.

remainingRisks: Wider vocabulary retains repetitive dictionary scaffolding; revised functional teaching is not a full editorial approval of that scaffold.
Room-number questions, hosting phrases and infinitive need have narrower new-context evidence than core case, agreement and permission contrasts.
Social replies use choices. Reading displays the text; writing is self-reviewed. Neither establishes spontaneous spoken interaction.
Two copied course returns provide opportunities, not proof of retention; mastery still requires unaided evidence across later visits.
